newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: ZIMBABWE MONEY RATES SEEN LOWER ON WORLD BANK AID.
newsitem.headline: ZIMBABWE MONEY RATES SEEN LOWER ON WORLD BANK AID.

text.p: Short-term trading rates on Zimbabwe's money market were mostly easier on Friday and dealers expected them to dip further after the World Bank said it would resume aid for the country's economic reform programme.
The dealers and some market analysts also said a slip in year-on-year inflation to 19.1 percent in July from 21.4 percent in June would also dampen the rates.
"We should see a continued drop in interest rates but I don't think it will be drastic because the chances of inflation rising again are still there," one dealer said.

The World Bank said on Thursday it was resuming crucial balance-of-payments support to Zimbabwe worth U.S.$62.5 million, two years after withholding such aid over the southern African country's failure to meet cost-cutting measures.
"This will obviously inject money into the system and rates should come down as the economy stabilises," one local money dealer said on Friday, adding however:
"But I think the central (Reserve) bank definitely will seek to tightly monitor the rates (by way of selling bills to mop up excess liquidity). They wouldn't like to see them drop too suddenly".
"I see the rates remaining in a narrow band between 23 and 25 percent or thereabouts," another dealer said.

The market opened on Friday with a surplus of Z$107 million, and the central bank, forecasting another surplus at the end of the day, auctioned Z$600 million worth of treasury bills to discount houses at 24.27 percent, down from Thursday's 24.47 percent.
NCDs maturing after 30, 60 and 90 days were being bought at 26.25 percent from 26.5 but sold firmer at 26 from 25 percent from 26 percent.
Bankers' acceptance bills were quoted lower at 25.25 from 25.5 percent (buying) but their selling rate edged up slightly to 25 from 24.5 percent. Call money shed one percentage point to 23 percent.
